concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: augmented reality
concepts.definition: Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.

defining_facts.text: Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
Augmented virtuality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state, opposite augmented reality, in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content.
Augmented reality (AR), unlike virtual reality (VR), does not require an immersive experience and instead emphasizes augmenting real-world content with digital content.
Augmented reality (AR) applications include archaeology, architecture, industrial manufacturing, commerce (particularly e-commerce), gaming, and medical domains, among other domains.
In archaeology, augmented reality (AR) can display things that are not visible to the naked eye on a screen and can reconstruct lost structures.
In industrial manufacturing, augmented reality (AR) can allow a person to see things while repairing or troubleshooting a component of an industrial setup.
The presence of many augmented reality (AR) applications in commerce, particularly e-commerce, is one motivation for the metaverse concept.
Pokemon Go is a famous augmented reality (AR) gaming application.

Augmented reality (AR) is defined by the Merriam-Webster dictionary as an enhanced version of reality created by the use of technology, primarily computer technology, to overlay digital information on an image of something being viewed through a device.

The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D.

An augmented reality (AR) system has four characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content such as image, video, or text; the enhancement is registered in 3D so that it appears at its appropriate place rather than randomly and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects; the enhancement is experienced through the user's sensory organs; and the system supports the user's interaction with the digital content in the enhanced environment rather than separately, giving the user the feel of being in reality at all times.

A system is identified as an augmented reality (AR) system by checking the four AR characteristics one by one, and it is an AR system only if all four are satisfied; if at least one characteristic is not satisfied, it is not an AR system.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.
An augmented reality (AR) system can superimpose extra information, such as non-existent furniture, as digital content over the real-world view of a room.

The dictionary definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a medium consisting of immersive computer-generated environments in which elements of physical and virtual environments are combined, but this definition is not categorical about how MR differs from virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR).

One definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR comprises everything in between the two extremes of the reality-virtuality continuum, the real environment and the virtual environment, so augmented reality (AR) is included in this broader definition of MR.

Another definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR denotes the capability to combine augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) technologies in the same application or on the same device, so such a combined application is called MR from a developer's point of view.

Another definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a strong version of augmented reality (AR), meaning a more capable version of augmented reality that has an advanced understanding of the physical environment and may be bound to specific hardware.

In one definition used by many people, mixed reality (MR) is a synonym for augmented reality (AR), because in both cases the user views reality augmented or enhanced with digital content overlaid on the view of reality, and can interact with that content.

Because most definitions of mixed reality (MR) are confusing and the controversy is not needed for this course, the course assumes that MR is the same technology as augmented reality (AR) and treats the two terms as interchangeable.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: head-mounted display
concepts.definition: A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.

defining_facts.text: The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

In the 1950s, especially toward the latter half of the decade, people started working on and considering different types of head-mounted displays (HMDs), a new kind of computer display that was less common than regular computer monitors.
In 1961, engineers at Philco Corporation developed an early head-mounted display (HMD) that could track users' motion but was bulky and uncomfortable to wear.
In 1965, Tom Furness and colleagues at the Wright-Patterson Air Force Base worked on visually coupled systems for pilots that consisted of head-mounted displays (HMDs).
In 1967, Sutherland developed the Sword of Damocles, a head-mounted display (HMD), and was the first to demonstrate an HMD with head tracking and computer-generated imagery.

In 1985, Scott Fisher and colleagues at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) developed and launched Virtual Visual Environment Display (VIVED), the first commercially viable and commercially available stereoscopic head-tracked head-mounted display (HMD) with a wide field of view.

The three broad types of visual displays are head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are wearable and mobile, world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and are stationary, and regular displays, which are mobile or can be stationary.
Although head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be used as input to track head motion, their primary use is as a display device.
A head-mounted display (HMD) is a sophisticated piece of equipment that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components within its package.

A head-mounted display (HMD) places images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens, with one screen providing monoscopic viewing and two screens providing stereoscopic viewing, and stereoscopic HMDs are more common than monoscopic HMDs.
Head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be further categorized into three types: non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through.

Non-see-through HMDs are typically used in virtual reality (VR), optical see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented reality (AR), and video see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented virtuality, in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.

concepts.name: virtual environment
concepts.definition: Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

defining_facts.text: A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

The artificial or synthetic environment of a virtual reality (VR) system is a computer-generated graphical representation of a real world or an imaginary or fantastic world, populated with artificial objects, and is not a real environment.

An artificial environment in a virtual reality (VR) system can recreate a real world using real-world imagery or video, as in a virtual tour, but it still counts as a virtual reality system because it is a computer-generated scenario and changes are not happening in real time.

The sensory experience characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system provides computer-generated stimuli to the user's sensory organs, such as eyes and ears, so the user can immersively experience the artificial or synthetic environment, and this immersive experience is a hallmark of a virtual reality system.

The user interaction characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system must be interactive: the user can act on or interact with elements in the environment, and user actions or inputs partially determine what happens in the environment, producing dynamic changes in the virtual environment, just as people interact with objects in the real world.

concepts.name: output device
concepts.definition: An output device is an XR hardware component that produces output to stimulate a user's sensory organs, not only a visual display; examples include visual displays, audio output, haptics, motion platforms, and treadmills.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).
In virtual reality (VR) hardware, a display or output device is used in a broad sense to mean any device that produces output that stimulates the user's sensory organs, not only a visual display.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the user's actions and positions are tracked by input devices and sent as input data; the input data is processed and the environment is rendered; the XR engine, as middleware, uses hardware resources to generate output data; and output devices stimulate the user's senses with that output.
A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller.
The display controller is responsible for image generation, meaning it creates a representation of a scene as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed on a two-dimensional screen.

A graphic display screen generally has a grid of picture elements, or pixels; when these pixels are activated, or excited, by an electrical or electromechanical means, they emit light with specific intensities that the viewer perceives as a colored image on the screen.

The video controller uses the data stored in video memory to render an image on the screen, converting the digital image into some analog voltages required to activate the pixels, and it controls the pixel excitation mechanism using the video memory content.

concepts.name: virtual reality headset
concepts.definition: Virtual reality headset is a wearable display that places a screen close to the eyes and uses a lens to focus the screen's light on the retina, making the screen appear as a virtual image.

defining_facts.text: In virtual reality (VR) headsets, light emitted from the displays reaches the retina and is guided by engineered lenses in the headset and natural lenses in the eye, a combined system that helps the user perceive immersive visual content.
Knowledge of how light propagates through lenses and the human eye is important for understanding how virtual reality (VR) headsets work and how they lead to visual perception.

A virtual reality (VR) headset places a screen very close to the eyes to fill the view and uses a convex lens, functioning like reading glasses, to focus the screen's light on the retina, after which normal eye operation takes over.

For the best experience, the screen in a virtual reality (VR) headset is placed at the focal length of its engineered lens, so that the screen appears to the user as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance.

In a virtual reality (VR) headset, even though the screen appears as a virtual image, a real image is nevertheless formed on the retina, and a person does not perceive the world unless real images are formed on the retina.

concepts.name: stereoscopic vision
concepts.definition: Stereoscopic vision is the perception of three-dimensional objects and space from left and right two-dimensional images processed simultaneously, aided by binocular vision.

defining_facts.text: In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

When the left and right two-dimensional (2D) images are processed simultaneously, the processing generates a three-dimensional (3D) view of the objects, so stereoscopic vision, which is aided by binocular vision, helps a person perceive three-dimensional objects.

concepts.name: field of view
concepts.definition: Field of view (FOV) is an angular measure of the region visible to the eye at a single point in time, and in virtual reality it is the amount of virtual environment visible.

defining_facts.text: Field of view (FOV) is a content-related factor in virtual reality (VR) that affects susceptibility to cybersickness (CS), and it is the extent to which the display in a VR headset captures the user's field of vision.
A larger field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) captures a larger field of vision and generally results in greater immersion.
Research has found that reducing the field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) can be an effective way to alleviate symptoms of cybersickness (CS).

An excessively narrow field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) can decrease immersion and increase head movement to look for things in the environment, which may exacerbate or increase cybersickness (CS); finding the optimal FOV is crucial for creating a comfortable VR experience.

Developer-side strategies for reducing cybersickness (CS) include field of view (FOV) adjustment, dynamic visual blur, rest frames, optical-flow manipulation, hardware-level alterations, and locomotion modifications.
Field of view (FOV) is the amount of virtual environment that is visible at any moment.
Field of view (FOV) adjustment can, ideally, mitigate the onset or severity of cybersickness (CS) because restricting the field of view reduces peripheral optical flow.
Field of view (FOV) adjustment has been found to be effective across genders without any negative impacts.

A drawback of field of view (FOV) adjustment is that it can reduce presence or sense of presence and impair performance in visual tasks because it restricts certain visual content, potentially degrading user experience.
A symmetric mask is a classical field of view (FOV) adjustment technique that occludes the periphery in reaction to translational and/or angular velocity, but it can affect presence.

An asymmetric mask is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy that is considered an adaptive restrictor because it obscures peripheral regions with higher optical flow during virtual locomotion while leaving regions with lower optical flow visible, so it adapts based on optical flow.

A side restrictor, described as an asymmetric mask, is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy that obscures only one side of the periphery during virtual rotation and laterally shifts the center of restriction in the direction of the turn, providing a controlled way of restriction.
A ground visible restrictor is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy in which the ground plane remains visible during movement.

Optical-flow manipulation is a cybersickness (CS) reduction technique that can involve visually mixing optical-flow patterns in the reverse direction of virtual visual motion, using a restricted field of view (FOV) aligned with optical flow, or reducing perceived optical flow by geometrical simplification of the virtual environment.
Field of view (FOV) is the view frustum, that is, the region visible to the human eye, and it is an angular measure of what can be seen at a single point in time.

The human eye has an approximately 180-degree horizontal field of view (FOV) and a 150-degree vertical field of view, and within the 180-degree horizontal range a person sees things using both central and peripheral vision.

concepts.name: human eye
concepts.definition: The human eye is the sense organ for vision that contains a cornea, iris, pupil, and natural lens and focuses visible light on the retina, where photoreceptors convert it into neural pulses sent to the brain.

defining_facts.text: Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye.
The material that makes up the cornea and the lens of the human eye refracts light so that images are focused on the retina.

The iris controls the amount of light entering the human eye by dilating or constricting the pupil, typically dilating it in dark surroundings to admit more light and constricting it in bright light to admit less.

The human eye contains two types of photoreceptors, rods and cones, in which rods are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina and cones are mainly located in the small central region of the retina called the fovea.

The human eye contains a cornea that acts as a powerful lens with fixed focal depth, a natural lens with variable focal depth, and a non-planar retina that is the image surface where light falls and is converted by photoreceptors into neural pulses transmitted to the brain through optical nerves.
Compared with an artificially created lens setup, the human eye has no focal plane as such; its non-planar, spherically curved retina replaces the focal plane.
The interior of the human eye is liquid, so after transmission through the lens light passes through liquid, whereas in an artificially created lens setup light passes through air after the lens.

In the human eye, a ray of light passes through five media before hitting the retina—air with refractive index 1.009, cornea with 1.376, aqueous fluid with 1.336, natural lens with 1.413, and vitreous fluid with 1.337—and each medium has its own refractive index.
Because the outer diameter of the human eyeball is approximately 24 millimeters, a single lens of at least 40 diopters would be required to converge parallel rays onto the center of the retina.

The human eye effectively contains two convex lenses, the cornea with optical power of approximately 40 diopters and the natural lens with approximately 20 diopters, so their combined optical power is about 60 diopters, which is sufficient to focus images of faraway objects onto the retina.

concepts.name: visual sense
concepts.definition: Visual sense is a human sense that has electromagnetic energy as its stimulus, photoreceptors as its receptors, and the eye as its sense organ.

defining_facts.text: The human senses classified by stimulus, receptor, and sense organ are vision (electromagnetic energy, photoreceptors, eye), auditory (air pressure waves, mechanoreceptors, ear), touch (tissue distortion, mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors, skin and muscles), balance (gravity or acceleration, mechanoreceptors, vestibular organs that act as sense organs), taste (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, mouth), and smell (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, nose).

concepts.name: photoreceptor
concepts.definition: Photoreceptor is a bodily sensor in the eye's retina that is activated only by visible light and converts visible light into neural pulses for visual perception.

defining_facts.text: The eyes contain photoreceptors, which are activated by electromagnetic energy in the frequency range of visible light and therefore target only visible light.

The retina at the back of the eye consists of photoreceptors, which are the bodily sensors required for visual perception, and optic nerve fibers, which are neurons that carry the signal to the brain.

The human eye contains two types of photoreceptors, rods and cones, in which rods are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina and cones are mainly located in the small central region of the retina called the fovea.

concepts.name: retina
concepts.definition: Retina is the non-planar image surface at the back of the eye where light falls and is converted by photoreceptors into neural pulses transmitted to the brain by optic nerve fibers.

defining_facts.text: Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye.
The material that makes up the cornea and the lens of the human eye refracts light so that images are focused on the retina.

The retina at the back of the eye consists of photoreceptors, which are the bodily sensors required for visual perception, and optic nerve fibers, which are neurons that carry the signal to the brain.

The human eye contains two types of photoreceptors, rods and cones, in which rods are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina and cones are mainly located in the small central region of the retina called the fovea.

The human eye contains a cornea that acts as a powerful lens with fixed focal depth, a natural lens with variable focal depth, and a non-planar retina that is the image surface where light falls and is converted by photoreceptors into neural pulses transmitted to the brain through optical nerves.
Compared with an artificially created lens setup, the human eye has no focal plane as such; its non-planar, spherically curved retina replaces the focal plane.

Because the outer diameter of the human eyeball is approximately 24 millimeters, a single lens of at least 40 diopters would be required to converge parallel rays onto the center of the retina.

The human eye effectively contains two convex lenses, the cornea with optical power of approximately 40 diopters and the natural lens with approximately 20 diopters, so their combined optical power is about 60 diopters, which is sufficient to focus images of faraway objects onto the retina.

A virtual reality (VR) headset places a screen very close to the eyes to fill the view and uses a convex lens, functioning like reading glasses, to focus the screen's light on the retina, after which normal eye operation takes over.

In a virtual reality (VR) headset, even though the screen appears as a virtual image, a real image is nevertheless formed on the retina, and a person does not perceive the world unless real images are formed on the retina.

concepts.name: lens
concepts.definition: A lens is an engineered part of a virtual reality headset or a natural part of the human eye that guides and refracts light so that images are focused on the retina.

defining_facts.text: Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye.
The material that makes up the cornea and the lens of the human eye refracts light so that images are focused on the retina.

concepts.name: cornea
concepts.definition: The cornea is a refracting medium in the human eye that acts as a powerful lens with fixed focal depth, helping focus incoming light onto the retina.

defining_facts.text: Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye.
The material that makes up the cornea and the lens of the human eye refracts light so that images are focused on the retina.

The human eye contains a cornea that acts as a powerful lens with fixed focal depth, a natural lens with variable focal depth, and a non-planar retina that is the image surface where light falls and is converted by photoreceptors into neural pulses transmitted to the brain through optical nerves.

In the human eye, a ray of light passes through five media before hitting the retina—air with refractive index 1.009, cornea with 1.376, aqueous fluid with 1.336, natural lens with 1.413, and vitreous fluid with 1.337—and each medium has its own refractive index.

The human eye effectively contains two convex lenses, the cornea with optical power of approximately 40 diopters and the natural lens with approximately 20 diopters, so their combined optical power is about 60 diopters, which is sufficient to focus images of faraway objects onto the retina.

concepts.name: aqueous humor
concepts.definition: Aqueous humor is an internal semi-liquid medium of the human eye that lies between the cornea and the pupil and through which light passes before reaching the retina.

defining_facts.text: Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye.

concepts.name: vitreous humor
concepts.definition: Vitreous humor is an internal semi-liquid medium in the human eye, between the lens and the retina, through which light passes before reaching the retina.

defining_facts.text: Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye.

concepts.name: central vision
concepts.definition: Central vision is one of the two types of human vision that requires the eyes to be focused and pointed straight at an object to perceive a sharp color image.

defining_facts.text: Human eyes support two types of vision, central vision and peripheral vision, because photoreceptor density across the retina varies greatly.
Central vision requires the eyes to be focused and pointed straight at an object to perceive a sharp color image.
Peripheral vision is better than central vision at detecting movement, but it does not provide effective color perception.

concepts.name: peripheral vision
concepts.definition: Peripheral vision is a type of human vision supported by the peripheral region of the retina, where photoreceptor density is lower, with lower rod density and very low cone density, and it detects movement better than central vision but does not provide effective color perception.

defining_facts.text: Human eyes support two types of vision, central vision and peripheral vision, because photoreceptor density across the retina varies greatly.

Peripheral vision is supported by the peripheral region of the retina, where rays entering the cornea from the sides land, rod density is lower and cone density is very low, and photoreceptor density is lower, with a mix of rods and an even lesser amount of cones.
Peripheral vision is better than central vision at detecting movement, but it does not provide effective color perception.

never_defined.name: screen
never_defined.definition: A screen is a display on which an image or content is shown so that a human can perceive it.

never_defined.name: two-dimensional image
never_defined.definition: A Two-dimensional image is a representation of a scene that can be presented by a display device and that stereoscopic vision can make a user perceive as a three-dimensional object or space.

never_defined.name: three-dimensional object
never_defined.definition: A three-dimensional object is an object perceived through stereoscopic vision from two-dimensional images or rendered at a tracked position in augmented reality.

never_defined.name: three-dimensional space
never_defined.definition: Three-dimensional space is the space with x, y, and z axes in which an object can have three translational and three rotational degrees of freedom.

never_defined.name: virtual reality display
never_defined.definition: A virtual reality display is a display, such as a head-mounted display.

never_defined.name: liquid-crystal display
never_defined.definition: Liquid-crystal display (LCD) is a display that, in an augmented reality system, can be moved over a piece of paper to allow a user to see virtual content.

never_defined.name: frame rate
never_defined.definition: Frame rate is the speed, or temporal resolution, at which display pixels change, and in immersive environments higher frame rates are preferred so that motion is perceived smoothly without jitter.

never_defined.name: x axis
never_defined.definition: X axis is one of the three axes in three-dimensional space along which translational degrees of freedom occur and around which rotation can take place.

never_defined.name: y axis
never_defined.definition: The Y axis is one of the three axes in three-dimensional space, along which an object can have translational degrees of freedom.

never_defined.name: z axis
never_defined.definition: The Z axis is one of the three axes in three-dimensional space along which an object can have translational degrees of freedom.

never_defined.name: yaw
never_defined.definition: Yaw is one of the three rotational degrees of freedom of an object in three-dimensional space, and head-mounted display sensors can detect it from head motion to change the view.

never_defined.name: roll
never_defined.definition: Roll is one of the three rotational degrees of freedom in three-dimensional space, along with yaw and pitch, and a head-mounted display can detect roll to infer input for changing the view.

never_defined.name: projector
never_defined.definition: A projector is a part of some augmented reality devices that is used to project images or graphical information onto physical objects or three-dimensional space.

never_defined.name: motion
never_defined.definition: Motion is perceived in a virtual world with respect to the degrees of freedom that are supported.

never_defined.name: photoreceptor density
never_defined.definition: Photoreceptor density is a basic physiological property that varies greatly across the retina, is lower in the peripheral region of the retina, and can directly impact engineering requirements for visual display hardware.

never_defined.name: optic nerve
never_defined.definition: The optic nerve is a nerve that transmits neural pulses from the retina to the brain.

never_defined.name: neural signal
never_defined.definition: A neural signal is a signal from the retina that is transmitted to the brain through optical nerves.

never_defined.name: focal depth
never_defined.definition: Focal depth is a property of a lens in the human eye, fixed in the cornea and variable in the natural lens.

never_defined.name: lens setup
never_defined.definition: A lens setup is an artificially created setup in which light passes through air after the lens and which has a focal plane.

never_defined.name: focal plane
never_defined.definition: Focal plane is a plane in an artificially created lens setup.

never_defined.name: medium
never_defined.definition: A medium is something that sound requires to propagate and that light passes through.

never_defined.name: refractive index
never_defined.definition: Refractive index is a value that a medium in the human eye has as a ray of light passes through it.

never_defined.name: diopter
never_defined.definition: A diopter is a unit used to express the optical power of lenses.

never_defined.name: convex lens
never_defined.definition: A convex lens is a lens used in the human eye and in a VR headset to focus light onto the retina.

never_defined.name: optical power
never_defined.definition: Optical power is a focusing property of the human eye's convex lenses, measured in diopters, whose combined value is sufficient to focus images of faraway objects onto the retina.

never_defined.name: engineered lens
never_defined.definition: An engineered lens is a lens in a virtual reality headset at whose focal length the screen is placed, so that the screen appears to the user as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance.

never_defined.name: focal length
never_defined.definition: Focal length is the position at which the screen of a virtual reality headset is placed relative to the headset's engineered lens for the best experience, so that the screen appears to the user as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance.

never_defined.name: virtual image
never_defined.definition: A virtual image is an image that appears to a user, as the screen of a virtual reality headset appears at an infinite distance, although a real image is formed on the retina.

never_defined.name: real image
never_defined.definition: A real image is, in a virtual reality headset, an image that is formed on the retina, and a person cannot perceive the world unless real images are formed on the retina.

never_defined.name: horizontal field of view
never_defined.definition: Horizontal field of view (FOV) is the horizontal range in which the human eye sees things.

never_defined.name: vertical field of view
never_defined.definition: The vertical field of view is a field of view of the human eye.

never_defined.name: left eye
never_defined.definition: The left eye is one of the two eyes in stereoscopy, the eye that processes the left image.

never_defined.name: right eye
never_defined.definition: The right eye is one of the two eyes used in binocular vision and stereoscopy, and it may see areas not seen by the left eye and, in stereoscopy, it processes the right image.

never_defined.name: depth perception
never_defined.definition: Depth perception is enhanced by binocular vision.

never_defined.name: three-dimensional view
never_defined.definition: A three-dimensional view is a view of objects that is generated by the simultaneous processing of left and right two-dimensional images.

never_defined.name: translational movement
never_defined.definition: Translational movement is a type of three-dimensional movement in a virtual world that is used for navigating in that world.

never_defined.name: rotational movement
never_defined.definition: Rotational movement is a type of movement in a 3D virtual world that is primarily used for moving at different angles along the translational axis.

never_defined.name: visual display hardware
never_defined.definition: Visual display hardware is display hardware whose engineering requirements can be directly impacted by basic physiological properties such as photoreceptor density.

never_defined.name: jitter
never_defined.definition: Jitter is a lack of smoothness in perceived display motion that temporal resolution must avoid.

never_defined.name: wearable display
never_defined.definition: A wearable display is a virtual reality headset or augmented reality head-mounted display in which a magnifying lens brings the display close to the eye.

never_defined.name: magnifying lens
never_defined.definition: A magnifying lens is a lens used in augmented reality (AR) head-mounted displays, virtual reality (VR) headsets, or other wearable displays to bring a display close to the eye.

never_defined.name: corrective mechanism
never_defined.definition: A corrective mechanism is used in virtual reality headsets to avoid or reduce aliasing or the screen door effect, including adjusting field of view, foveated rendering techniques, and other ways of rendering content, in addition to increasing spatial resolution.

never_defined.name: foveated rendering
never_defined.definition: Foveated rendering is a corrective rendering technique that is used to avoid or reduce aliasing or the screen door effect in virtual reality headsets.

never_defined.name: motion perception
never_defined.definition: Motion perception is an immersive-environment case for which temporal resolution in a virtual reality headset requires frame rates much higher than ordinary television or movie standards, with higher frame rates preferred.
